h1: Moving from a lab job in pharma to brewery QC
title: Moving from a Pharma Lab to Brewery QC | Craft Beer School
desc: How a pharma lab background transfers into brewery quality control in India, the tests you will run and what is genuinely different about beer.
teaser: Pharma labs teach discipline. Brewery labs add yeast, sensory panels and beer that changes in the bottle.
standfirst: Pharma lab experience is one of the strongest backgrounds for brewery quality control. Good documentation, calibrated instruments and method discipline all carry straight across. The adjustment is learning beer's chemistry, its microbes and the role of taste.
sections: Your lab discipline is the main asset

Pharma labs run on good laboratory practice: written methods, calibrated instruments, traceable samples and records that would survive an audit. Many breweries, especially smaller ones, are still building that discipline. A QC analyst who brings it can raise a brewery's quality quickly.

Skills that carry over almost unchanged include pipetting, weighing, solution preparation, instrument calibration, sample management, out-of-specification investigations and document control. If you have worked under GMP, you already understand why a test that was not recorded effectively did not happen.
The tests are different but familiar

Brewery QC uses many of the same instrument types with different methods. Typical routine tests include:

  • Gravity and alcohol: by density meter or hydrometer.
  • pH: wort and beer, with a calibrated meter.
  • Bitterness: in bitterness units, usually by solvent extraction and UV spectrophotometry at 275 nm.
  • Colour: on the EBC or SRM scale by spectrophotometer.
  • Dissolved oxygen and carbon dioxide: in packaged beer.
  • Microbiology: plating on selective media to detect wild yeast and spoilage bacteria such as lactic acid bacteria.

Standard methods come from the ASBC and the EBC rather than a pharmacopoeia. The logic is the same. Read the method, follow it exactly and record everything.

In pharma you may have aimed for sterility. In a brewery the product is full of living yeast by design. The question is not whether microbes are present but whether the wrong ones are. Brewery micro work looks for beer spoilers: lactic acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Pediococcus, acetic acid bacteria and wild yeasts including diastaticus strains that can over-carbonate packaged beer.

Plates often need several days of incubation, so results trail the batch. Learning which samples to take and when, from yeast slurry to bright beer to filled packs, is a core part of the job. Our guide on becoming a yeast lab technician goes deeper into the yeast side.
Sensory is a lab test too

The biggest surprise for many pharma analysts is that taste counts as data. Breweries run sensory panels that check beer for off-flavours and true-to-type character. A beer can pass every instrument test and still be rejected because it tastes of diacetyl, which is buttery, or oxidised, which is papery.

Treat sensory training as you would any method validation. Learn the reference flavours, take part in panels and record your results. Panellists are always opt-in and tastings use small samples with spit cups available. You do not have to be a heavy beer drinker to be a good panellist. Careful attention matters far more than habit.

A tablet is stable on the shelf. Beer is not. Oxygen picked up at packaging, heat in transport and light through clear or green glass all change its flavour over weeks. In much of India, storage temperatures can run well above 30 °C in summer, which speeds staling.

Brewery QC therefore includes shelf life work: holding samples, sometimes at raised temperature to simulate ageing, then tasting them over time. Pharma analysts familiar with stability studies will recognise the idea, even though the end point here is flavour rather than assay.

Lead with method discipline, instrument experience and documentation. Mention any microbiology, HPLC or GC work, as larger breweries use chromatography for flavour compounds. Then show you have done your homework on beer: name the routine brewery tests, explain why dissolved oxygen matters and say you understand the role of sensory panels.

Visit a brewery if you can and ask to see their lab. Even a small brewpub lab with a pH meter, a microscope and an incubator will tell you a lot. Our guide on shift work at a large brewery describes the environment you would support.

Learn the brewing process end to end before your interview, at least to the level of explaining what happens at each stage and which test checks it. Then write a one page sampling plan for a small brewery: what to test, where and how often, from wort through to filled cans. That page shows a hiring manager you can translate pharma discipline into beer.
faqs: Is pharma lab experience useful in brewery QC?
Very. Good laboratory practice, calibrated instruments, documentation and method discipline carry over almost unchanged and are valued by breweries.
What tests does a brewery QC lab run?
Gravity, alcohol, pH, bitterness, colour, dissolved oxygen, carbon dioxide and microbiology on selective media, plus sensory panels.
Do I need to drink beer to work in brewery QC?
No heavy drinking is needed. Sensory panels use small samples with spit cups and are opt-in. Careful attention matters more than habit.
How is brewery microbiology different from pharma?
Beer contains yeast by design, so the aim is to detect the wrong microbes, such as lactic acid bacteria and wild yeast, rather than achieve sterility.
